name: Arthashastra
info: The Arthashastra, or Kautilya's Arthashastra, is an ancient Indian Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, politics, economic policy and military strategy, compiled and revised over centuries and most likely complete between the 1st and 3rd century CE.

facts.made: Several authors over centuries; according to Olivelle, separate source treatises of 150 BCE to 50 CE, a compilation by a person named Kautilya in 50 to 125 CE and a major redaction between 175 and 300 CE; tradition names Chanakya, the counsellor of Chandragupta Maurya
facts.form: A Sanskrit treatise, mostly prose with a verse at the end of each chapter, in 15 books, 150 chapters and 180 topics, with about 5,300 sentences on politics, governance and war, apart from the table of contents and the epilogue
facts.where: Manuscripts include a palm-leaf copy given to the Mysore Oriental Library, a Malayalam-script manuscript in the Bavarian State Library and a Devanagari manuscript in a Jain library at Patan, Gujarat; early fragments come from sites in China, Afghanistan and Pakistan
facts.known: Statecraft and the duties of a king; the sage king; the network of spies; the six-fold policy and the Mandala theory; a mixed economy with taxes and state superintendents; civil and criminal law; the identification with Chanakya and its rejection by scholars

t: The Arthashastra is a compilation of earlier treatises, revised over centuries, which covers government, law, taxes, trade, spies, diplomacy and war.
Tradition ascribes it to Chanakya, counsellor of Chandragupta Maurya, but studies since 1965 have mostly rejected this, pointing to several authors and to details that fit the first centuries CE.
Thought lost by colonial-era scholars, it was identified in 1905 in the Mysore Oriental Library and published by R. Shamasastry in 1909.
dyk: The text advises that in areas struck by famine, epidemic or war the king should start public projects such as irrigation works and forts, and exempt those affected from taxes. It also recommends feeding horses and elephants that are too old, sick or injured to work.
ev: On Olivelle's dating, the oldest layer, separate treatises by separate authors, begins to be written, between 150 BCE and 50 CE
The Kautilya Recension, probably titled Dandaniti, is compiled between 50 and 125 CE on Olivelle's dating
The Spitzer Manuscript, found near Kizil in China, carries verses of the Arthashastra
The Shastric Redaction, the text as it exists today, is made between 175 and 300 CE on Olivelle's dating
A palm-leaf manuscript given to the Mysore Oriental Library is identified by Rudrapatna Shamasastry as the Arthashastra
Shamasastry publishes the Sanskrit text, followed by the first English translation in 1915
R. P. Kangle publishes a critical edition based on all the available manuscripts
The Arthashastra is inscribed in the UNESCO memory register at the 11th General Meeting of the Memory of the World Committee for Asia and the Pacific

sections.origins:
The Arthashastra, in full Kautilya's Arthashastra, is an ancient Indian Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, politics, economic policy and military strategy. It does not present itself as wholly new. At its start it states that it was composed by drawing together the Arthashastras of former teachers, and it names schools with different views on how many fields of knowledge are necessary, those of Brihaspati, Usanas and Manu, before setting out its own as the school of Kautilya. Rangarajan notes that the science of artha, material well-being, livelihood and wealth, was not developed by Kautilya but drew on older works that are all lost, and that Kautilya's is the earliest text of the kind to have come down. One possible reason for the loss of those works is that Kautilya's comprehensive treatise made them redundant, a possibility Olivelle also mentions.

Artha is one of the four aims of human life in Hinduism, the others being dharma, kama and moksha, and the Sanskrit title can be translated as a treatise on political science, economic science or simply statecraft. Scholars render it differently: Kangle as the science of the means to artha, Kosambi as the science of material gain, Boesche as the science of political economy and Olivelle as the science of politics. The text was influenced by Hindu texts such as the sections on kings, governance and legal procedures in the Manusmriti.
sections.content:
The Arthashastra is divided into 15 books, 150 chapters and 180 topics. The books deal with the training of a king, the activities of superintendents, civil law, the eradication of thorns, which is criminal law, secret conduct, the basis of the circle of states, the sixfold strategy, calamities, the king's march into battle, war, conduct toward confederacies, the weaker king, the capture of forts, esoteric practices and the organisation of a scientific treatise. The second book, on superintendents, is the largest, with 1,285 sentences, and the eleventh the smallest, with 56.

The text holds that there are four necessary fields of knowledge: the Vedas, the Anvikshaki or science of reasoning, the science of government and the science of economics, called Varta, which covers agriculture, cattle and trade. Without government, it says, disorder rises as in the proverb of the law of fishes, where the strong swallow the weak. The best king is the Raja-rishi, the sage king, who controls his senses, keeps learning and promotes the welfare of his people; his greatest enemies are lust, anger, greed, conceit, arrogance and foolhardiness. Other parts treat the screening of ministers, the network of spies, the three kinds of war, which are open, covert and silent, foreign policy with its six-fold policy and Mandala theory, taxes, a court system, marriage laws, forests and the care of animals.
sections.making:
Olivelle states that the surviving manuscripts are the product of a transmission with at least three major overlapping layers. By his account, the oldest layer, the sources of the Kautilya, dates from 150 BCE to 50 CE and consists of separate treatises by separate authors. The Kautilya Recension was made in 50 to 125 CE by a historical person named Kautilya, who compiled selections from them into a new shastra, probably titled Dandaniti. A major Shastric Redaction followed between 175 and 300 CE. Its author knew the Dharmashastras well, added the division into books and chapters and several books, expanded short statements into dialogues, and brought the text closer to Brahmanical social ideology; it was this redactor who made an Arthashastra out of a Dandaniti. McClish dates the Dandaniti to the first century BCE and its redaction possibly to the third century CE, by an author who called himself Kautilya.

Others differ. Kangle held that no substantial part could be assigned to a later age, Schlingloff thought the compendium arose in the first half of the first millennium CE, Scharfe dated the extant text to c. 150 CE and Trautmann proposed 250 CE for the compilation, after a statistical analysis of its words that found several authors. The text names its compiler Kautilya or Kautalya, a gotra name, and a verse at its end names Vishnugupta; scholars disagree over how these relate to Chanakya.
sections.reception:
The Arthashastra was influential until the 12th century, when it disappeared. Gupta-era and medieval texts, among them the Mudrarakshasa, the Panchatantra and Kamandaka's Nitisara, identify Kautilya or Vishnugupta with Chanakya, and the Manu Dharmashastra of the 2nd century CE appears to have used the earlier Dandaniti. Scholars hold that this identification began under the Guptas, who presented themselves as heirs of the Mauryas. Its basis is a verse that scholars regard as a later interpolation, in a text from which the name Chanakya is absent. Trautmann and McClish add that Indian nationalists saw in the text evidence of a pragmatic tradition of self-rule, and that scholars short of sources for the Mauryan era were reluctant to give up using it.

Scholars of the text raise anachronisms against a Mauryan date: Chinese silk, coral from Alexandria, Greek loan-words, the use of Sanskrit in edicts, the Roman dinara in a text that refers to it, and wooden fortifications at Pataliputra, which the text forbids. Max Weber wrote in 1919 that compared with it Machiavelli's The Prince is harmless; later scholars disagreed, noting its concern for the security and prosperity of the people and for the weak and poor. Boesche called it a bureaucratic welfare state with an extensive spy system, a view Trautmann challenged, finding a regulated market with private property. Shiv Shankar Menon called it a realist manual on running a state.
sections.survival:
Colonial-era scholars considered the text lost until 1905, when a palm-leaf copy in Sanskrit, presented by a Tamil Brahmin from Thanjavur to the newly opened Mysore Oriental Library headed by Benjamin Lewis Rice, was identified by the librarian Rudrapatna Shamasastry as the Arthashastra. He published English translations in instalments in the Indian Antiquary and the Mysore Review between 1905 and 1909, the Sanskrit text in 1909 and a first English translation in book form in 1915. Julius Jolly and Richard Schmidt published a new edition in 1923 and 1924, based on a Malayalam-script manuscript in the Bavarian State Library. In the 1950s fragments of a north Indian version came to light in a Devanagari manuscript in a Jain library at Patan, Gujarat, on which Muni Jina Vijay based an edition in 1959. R. P. Kangle published a critical edition in 1960.

Earlier evidence has also been found. Dozens of its verses appear on fragments from ancient Buddhist monasteries in northwest China, Afghanistan and northwest Pakistan, among them the Spitzer Manuscript of c. 200 CE from near Kizil and the birch-bark scrolls of the Bajaur Collection, of the 1st to 2nd century CE, found in 1999 at a site in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Olivelle states that revisions, errors, additions and perhaps subtractions have occurred since the final redaction of 300 CE or earlier.
sections.legacy:
The Arthashastra has been translated and studied by Shamasastry, Kangle, Rangarajan, Olivelle and McClish, among others. Olivelle called translating its dense, coded Sanskrit the most difficult translation project he had undertaken, and parts of the text remain opaque after a century of modern scholarship. Richard Davis wrote that Olivelle's translation of 2013 clearly supplants all earlier English ones, including those of Kangle and Rangarajan. McClish published The History of the Arthasastra in 2019, and Olivelle and McClish edited a selection of its texts in 2012.

Writers have drawn different lessons from it. Boesche, relying on Kangle's translation, called it a great political book of the ancient world. Sihag reads it as a treatise on economic development that stresses the proper measurement of economic performance and ethics as the glue binding a society. On the war it recommends, scholars note that it prefers peace where progress would be equal, since war brings losses, expenses and absence from home, while allowing assassination, discord and propaganda as means of winning one, and humane treatment of the conquered afterwards. On 5 November 2026 the text was inscribed in the UNESCO memory register at the 11th General Meeting of the Memory of the World Committee for Asia and the Pacific.

summary: The Arthashastra is a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, law, economics and war that tradition ascribes to Chanakya. Scholars such as Olivelle and McClish see a compilation of earlier works revised over centuries, completed between the 1st and 3rd century CE; it was lost, then identified in 1905.
references: Roger Boesche, The First Great Political Realist: Kautilya and His Arthashastra (Lexington, 2002)
R. P. Kangle, Kautilya Arthashastra, Part III (Motilal Banarsidass, 1965)
Mark McClish, The History of the Arthasastra (Cambridge University Press, 2019)
Patrick Olivelle, King, Governance, and Law in Ancient India: Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra (Oxford University Press, 2013)
notes: The article's reference and sources lists are empty in the saved text, so references are left empty.

Dates are disputed and given as each scholar gives them: Olivelle 150 BCE to 300 CE in three phases, McClish 1st century BCE and possibly 3rd century CE, Scharfe c. 150 CE, Trautmann 250 CE, Kangle Mauryan. start -150 follows Olivelle's oldest layer.

The article says the text was influential until the 12th century and also says its influence in Asian history rests on the misidentification with Chanakya; I gave only the first and the Gupta-era identification.
The article gives Olivelle's final redaction as 300 CE or earlier, and the Shastric Redaction as 175 to 300 CE; both are used as stated.
The sentence on the 11th General Meeting and the UNESCO listing is repeated in the article, in the section on structure; it is dated 5 November 2026 as the article has it.

Left out: the popular-culture list; the Gujarat origin argument (Burrow); abortion and marriage-law details; the Boesche and Menon quotations beyond summary; the article's text on forests and wildlife apart from the care of old animals.
The article contradicts itself on the Dandaniti spelling (Dandanati/Dandaniti) and on whether the Panchatantra is of 300 CE; I used Dandaniti and did not date the Panchatantra.
